title: A Heart for God’s Word
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro

outline.title: The Centrality of Scripture
subpoints: Psalm 119 is located near the physical center of the Bible
The Psalm emphasizes the centrality of God's Word in Christian life
Reformation principle: Scripture alone is sufficient for faith and life

outline.title: Human Need and Divine Solution
subpoints: Human nature and sin remain constant across ages
The true need of man is the God revealed in Scripture
Revival comes through repentance and knowing God's Word

outline.title: The Subject of the Psalm
subpoints: The dual focus on the Word of God and the God of the Word
Consensus among commentators on the theme
The frequency of references to Scripture in the text

outline.title: Terminology for God's Word
subpoints: Eight distinct Hebrew terms used to describe Scripture
Examples include Law (Torah), Testimonies, Precepts, and Statutes
Each term highlights a different aspect of God's revelation

outline.title: Literary Structure
subpoints: Each stanza of eight verses begins with a consecutive letter of the Hebrew alphabet
A masterpiece of Hebrew poetry and divine inspiration

summary:
This sermon introduces a 23-part series on Psalm 119, focusing on the first eight verses. The speaker highlights the unique position of Psalm 119 near the center of the Bible, symbolizing the centrality of Scripture in the life of a believer. Drawing on Reformation theology, particularly the views of John Calvin and James Boyce, the message emphasizes the doctrine of *sola scriptura*, asserting that the Bible alone is sufficient for faith and life, and that true revival stems from the proclamation of God's Word rather than cultural trends or entertainment.

The sermon addresses the unchanging nature of human sin and the consistent need for divine revelation. It argues that while culture fades, the Word of God abides forever, serving as the ultimate solution to humanity's spiritual plight. The speaker outlines the plan to cover the entire psalm over several months, preaching through the text verse by verse in both morning and afternoon services.

Finally, the message provides an introductory analysis of the psalm's structure and vocabulary. It identifies the psalm as an acrostic poem, where each stanza begins with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet. The speaker details the eight different Hebrew terms used within the first eight verses to refer to God's Word, such as 'Law,' 'Testimonies,' and 'Statutes,' illustrating the richness and multifaceted nature of biblical revelation.
